transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi Doctor. Well, to be honest, it’s my head. It just feels so... cloudy lately, and it’s driving me absolutely up the wall. I manage a few community associations—condos, HOAs, that sort of thing—and I’ve been doing it for a long time. I didn’t get past junior high, but I worked my way up and I know my properties inside and out, so I'm used to being on top of everything. 

But lately, I’ll be sitting at my desk, and I’ll pull up a board packet for the monthly meeting, or maybe it’s just a simple email from a vendor, like the landscaping guys asking about a broken sprinkler, and I just... I just stare at it. I stare and stare. It’s like I cannot decide on even the simplest things. Normally, I’d just fire off a reply—boom, approved, get it done. I used to handle all of this so fast, just juggling fifty things at once without breaking a sweat. 

But now, it’s like my brain is wading through thick mud. I just sit there looking at the words on the screen, and I can't figure out what to do next, which isn't like me at all. I mean, the board members rely on me to make these calls, and if I can't even tell a plumber to fix a leak without agonizing over it for an hour... it just really slows everything down. And it's frustrating, you know? To have your mind just sort of stall out on you when you're just trying to get through a normal Tuesday morning. It's just this heavy, cloudy feeling that won't lift, and I really need to get back to working the way I used to.
Besides this mental cloudiness, have you noticed feeling persistently sad, down, or having lost interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy?

Well, yes, actually. Now that you mention it, it’s not just the work stuff. It’s... it’s everything, really. I just don't have the energy or the... the desire for it. Like, I’ve been taking this salsa dancing class at the community center for, gosh, it has to be three or four years now. Every Thursday evening, rain or shine. I’ve always loved it. The music, the movement, getting to chat with the other ladies before class starts. But lately, when Thursday rolls around, I just think about getting dressed and driving over there, and it feels like climbing a mountain. So I just stay home. I haven't been in weeks. 

And it's the same with the art galleries downtown. Usually, on a Saturday afternoon, I love to just stroll through and look at the new pieces. I don't buy much, but I just like seeing what the local artists are up to, you know? The colors and the creativity. But the thought of doing that now just... it does nothing for me. It feels pointless. 

Even Sunday dinners. I’ve always cooked a big Sunday meal for my kids and grandkids. A big roast, or maybe a lasagna from scratch, with all the sides. It’s a whole production, and it’s usually the highlight of my week, having everyone around the big table, laughing and talking over each other. But the last few Sundays, I’ve just ordered pizzas. I couldn't bring myself to plan a menu, go to the grocery store, stand in the kitchen for hours... I just didn't care. And that's what scares me the most, I think. Not caring about the things that usually make me feel like me. It's just this heavy, flat feeling all the time.
How long have you been feeling this way—this cloudiness, low energy, and loss of interest in things you used to enjoy?

Well, let me think... it hasn't been forever, but it feels like it, you know? The really noticeable part—this heavy cloud, the total lack of energy, and just losing my spark and my confidence—that’s been going on for about two weeks now. Exactly two weeks, actually. I know exactly when it started because it was right around the time my husband, Richard, officially retired. 

He worked at the auto plant for almost forty years, God bless him, and they had this big retirement dinner for him on a Friday. And then Monday rolled around, and suddenly... he was just there. In the house. All day. Every day. And don't get me wrong, I love the man, we've been married a long time, but having him constantly underfoot while I'm trying to work from my home office... it just shifted everything. At first, I thought I was just annoyed that my routine was disrupted, you know? He'd come in asking where the good coffee filters were while I was trying to review a vendor contract, and I'd just lose my train of thought. 

But then it turned into this... this sharper change. It wasn't just being annoyed anymore. It was like all the air went out of my tires. I started doubting myself on things I’ve done a million times. I'd look at a budget for the Oak Creek HOA, and suddenly I didn't trust my own math, which is ridiculous because I've managed their books for a decade. And then the energy just plummeted. That's when the Sunday dinners stopped, and the salsa dancing... it all just kind of cascaded right after he hung up his hard hat. So, yes, it's been about a solid two weeks of feeling like this completely different, bogged-down version of myself. It's just so strange how it all happened right when he came home for good.
Along with the low mood and cloudiness, have you also been feeling unusually anxious, worried, or on edge during this time?

Anxious? No, I wouldn't say anxious. I mean, I'm not sitting here biting my nails or pacing the floors, you know? It's not that sort of nervous, jittery feeling where you're just waiting for the other shoe to drop. Like, I remember when my daughter was first learning to drive, oh, ages ago now, but I'd sit by the window just wringing my hands, totally on edge until she pulled back into the driveway. That was anxiety. This isn't like that at all. 

It's really just... flat. Like I said, it's that heavy, muddy feeling. I'm not worried about the HOA budgets, I just... can't bring myself to care about them, or I just stare at them and my brain won't work. If I were anxious, I think I'd be fretting over every little mistake, calling the vendors three times to make sure they got my email. But instead, I'm just looking at the screen and feeling like I'm underwater. 

Even with Richard being home all the time now, which, like I mentioned, was a huge adjustment. You'd think I'd be worried about him getting in the way or us driving each other crazy, but it's more like I just don't have the energy to even be properly annoyed anymore. He'll ask me where the remote is for the TV in the den, and I just sort of look at him. I don't feel that spike of irritation or worry about my day being derailed, I just feel... nothing. Or just tired. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm on edge or worried. It's really just the opposite. It's like all the edges have been smoothed out into this big, gray blur, and I'm just stuck in the middle of it.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep or appetite since this started two weeks ago?

Well, the sleep is... it's about the same, I suppose. I've never been a fantastic sleeper, what with my age and the aches and pains that come with it, but it hasn't gotten terribly worse. But the eating... now that you mention it, yes, my appetite has been completely out of whack since Richard retired and this whole heavy feeling started. 

Usually, I'm a three-square-meals-a-day kind of woman. I’d have my oatmeal with berries in the morning, a nice salad or half a sandwich for lunch while I’m working on the HOA files, and then a proper dinner. But lately? I just don't even think about food. It's like the hunger signal in my brain just got switched off. I'll get up, pour myself a cup of coffee, and maybe take a few bites of toast, and then... nothing. I just sit at my desk, staring at the computer, and the coffee just sort of carries me through the whole afternoon. I don't even realize I haven't eaten until Richard comes in around five asking what's for dinner, and of course, like I told you, I haven't been cooking.

And the strange thing is, even when I do finally eat something in the evening, it's not a real meal. I just end up picking at things. We always have a bag of flour tortillas in the pantry, so I'll just tear off pieces of a plain tortilla while I'm sitting in front of the television. Or I'll find a box of those little powdered donuts Richard likes, and I'll eat three or four of those. But I'm not even enjoying them! It's not like I'm having a craving for sweets or anything. It's just... mindless chewing, I guess. I don't taste it, I don't get any satisfaction from it, it's just something to put in my mouth because I know I probably should eat something. It's just so unlike me. I used to love food, love cooking it, love sitting down to enjoy it. And now, a cup of coffee and a handful of plain tortillas is basically all I can manage for the whole day.
Have you had any thoughts of worthlessness, excessive guilt, or thoughts about death or that life isn't worth living during these past two weeks?

Oh, heavens no, nothing about dying or anything like that. I mean, I know I'm feeling awful and bogged down, but I'm certainly not looking to leave this earth anytime soon. Lord knows Richard wouldn't even know how to turn on the washing machine if I did, bless his heart. So no, life is still worth living, I'm just having a hard time living it right this minute. 

But... the guilt. That's a whole different story. I have just been absolutely eaten up with it. It’s this awful, nagging feeling that I’m just... useless lately. Especially with the Oak Creek properties. You see, right before this whole fog rolled in and Richard came home for good, we had our quarterly resident meeting. And I was standing there in the clubhouse, and some of the folks—like Mr. Abernathy in unit 12, he’s always very vocal, and Mrs. Higgins who always worries about the curb appeal—they were asking about getting the guest parking lot repaved and maybe putting in some new landscaping by the front gates. 

And I just... I don't know what came over me, but I started speaking way too big. I was standing there promising things, telling them, "Oh sure, we can get that done this spring, no problem at all, we'll make it look beautiful." I was just so confident in the moment. But I did all that talking before I even sat down to check the money. I didn't look at the reserve funds or the operating budget first to see if we actually had the padding for it. 

And now that I'm in this... this slump, I just keep looking at the computer screen, when I can actually bring myself to focus on it, and I keep thinking I completely let the residents down. I feel so terrible about it, just sick with myself for being so careless. I mean, I've managed these books for ten years! I don't have a fancy college degree, but I know my numbers, and I should know better than to open my mouth and make promises without the ledger right in front of me. 

The silly thing is, nobody has even called to complain. Not Mr. Abernathy, not the board president, nobody. Nobody has said I ruined anything or that I made a mess of the accounts. They probably haven't even thought twice about that meeting. But in my head? I just sit there chewing on my pieces of tortilla, staring at the wall, thinking about how I let them all down and how I'm just a fraud who is no good at this job anymore. It just weighs on me so heavy, this feeling that I'm just worthless to them now because I spoke out of turn. It just loops and loops in my mind all afternoon.

Have you noticed any moments during these two weeks when you felt even a little better or more like yourself—for example, when Richard was out of the house or you had some time alone—or has this heavy, flat feeling stayed constant no matter what you're doing or who's around?

Well, you know, you'd think so, wouldn't you? Because normally, I am a woman who cherishes her quiet time. But... no. It really hasn't lifted at all, not even for a minute. 

Just the other day, actually, Richard did go out. He decided he needed to go down to the Home Depot—he’s got it in his head now that he’s retired that he’s going to build a birdhouse or a feeder or something, which, Lord help us, the man has never been handy a day in his life. But he went, and he took the truck, and he was gone for a good three hours because he always ends up talking the ear off the poor folks in the lumber aisle. 

So there I was, all by myself in the house. The television was finally off, nobody was asking me where the good scissors were or what we were doing for lunch. Just absolute peace and quiet. And I thought to myself, well, maybe now I'll feel a little spark. Maybe I'll get up and put a load of towels in the wash, or at least feel a little relief, a little breathing room, you know? 

But... nothing. I just sat there at the kitchen table with my cold coffee. I didn't even turn on the radio like I usually do when I have the house to myself. The quiet didn't make me feel any lighter, and him being gone didn't make a lick of difference. It's just exactly like I told you, that heavy, muddy feeling. It just sits right on my chest from the minute I wake up till the minute I finally go to sleep. 

It really doesn't seem to matter if the sun is shining, or if Richard is out of my hair, or if the house is perfectly quiet. It's just... constant. Like a thick fog that just won't burn off, no matter what time of day it is or who is or isn't in the room with me. I used to love having the house to myself, I'd put on my slippers and putter around, maybe wipe down the baseboards or water the pothos plants... but now, it just doesn't matter. The environment changes, but I don't. It's all just the exact same gray blur.
Have you ever had a period like this before—weeks of feeling this low, foggy, and uninterested in things—at any earlier point in your life, even years ago?

Well... if I'm being completely honest, and I suppose I have to be if we're going to figure this out... yes. I have. It’s not something I really talked about with anyone, certainly not with Richard, but if I really sit and look back over the calendar, these... well, these depressed stretches, they’ve actually been coming back on and off for about a year now. 

Just these patches where I'd get so bogged down and foggy for a few weeks at a time. I remember last fall, right around when we were doing the annual budget review for the complex and getting the gutters checked, I had a spell where I just felt so low and couldn't care less about the reserve funds, which is practically a sin in my line of work! I didn't say a word to anyone, I just thought, well, maybe I'm just getting old, or maybe it's the weather turning cold, you know how it gets in November. And then it would sort of lift eventually, and I'd go back to my files and my morning oatmeal and feel fine again. It would just come and go like that, maybe every few months or so over this past year. 

But this latest one, the one I'm in right now... it feels different. It really feels tied directly to what happened after my husband stopped working. When Richard officially retired two weeks ago and started being home all day, every day, pacing around the kitchen and asking me about lunch when I'm trying to look at the HOA ledgers... that's when this current fog rolled in. It's like his retirement just flipped a switch and brought it all crashing down on me. All those other times over the past year, I could sort of quietly wait them out, but this time, with him being home for good, it just feels so much heavier and more permanent than those other stretches.

Thinking back to those earlier low, foggy spells over the past year—like the one last fall—about how many days or weeks would each one typically last, and were they severe enough to actually interfere with your ability to manage the HOA work and daily activities?

Well, if I'm really sitting down and measuring it out, I'd say those spells last fall and over the winter, they'd usually stick around for maybe two or three weeks at a time. Sometimes a little longer if things were particularly stressful around the property, but right around that two to three-week mark is usually when the fog would finally start to thin out just a little bit. 

And as for the work... well, it's a bit of a mixed bag, if I'm being completely honest with you. Because I am not the type of woman to just abandon my post, you understand? I've never been one to just call in sick and pull the covers over my head. So I am still getting to work. I make sure I am sitting at that desk in the clubhouse every single morning, rain or shine, just like I always have. 

But... well, the actual doing of the work? That's where it all gets so sticky and difficult. I have had to slow down my decisions to an absolute crawl. Normally, I can look at an invoice from the landscaping crew or the pool maintenance folks and just know right away if it's correct, sign on the dotted line, and move on to the next thing. But right now? And during those other spells? I just do not trust my judgment right now. Not one bit. I'm so terrified of making another mistake or promising something we can't afford. 

So I've been having to call my assistant over—she's a sweet girl, just started with us not too long ago, and she's still learning the ropes—but I have to ask her to double-check all the vendor details for me. I'll have her look over the invoices and the master contracts just to make sure the numbers match up, because my brain just feels too muddy to catch anything, and I keep second-guessing every single digit I look at. 

And the board... oh, the board always has a million things they want approved yesterday. But I've actually had to put off a couple of board items completely. They wanted to review the bids for the new security gates, and I just... I couldn't do it. I just pushed the folders to the side of my desk and told them we'd have to revisit it at the next meeting. I just can't bring myself to make a final call on anything important because I'm so scared I'll ruin the accounts or steer them wrong. So I'm there, physically, sitting in my chair, but I'm just barely keeping the wheels turning. I just have no faith in myself to do it right.

Have you ever had a period—lasting several days or more—where you felt unusually energetic, elated, or 'on top of the world,' needed much less sleep than usual, or found yourself talking faster or taking on more risks than normal?

Well, now that you say that... yes, I suppose there have been times like that. It's funny you bring it up, because I was just thinking the other day about how different I feel now compared to... well, there were these days, maybe a little while back, where I felt almost, I don't know, almost too bright, if that makes any sense. Just bold as brass, like I had a fire lit under me. 

I remember going into the association meetings—and usually, you know, I'm the one trying to keep the peace, keeping everyone strictly to the agenda because these board members, Lord love them, they will argue for an hour about the color of the playground mulch if you let them. But during those particular days, I was the one doing all the talking. I was just talking right over people, which really isn't like me at all. Mrs. Henderson was trying to read a complaint about the visitor parking rules, and I just cut right across her, bold as you please, and told her exactly how we were going to handle it and why her idea wouldn't work. I just felt so sharp, like my brain was moving a mile a minute and I just didn't have the patience to wait for anyone else to catch up. 

But the thing is, it wasn't always a fun feeling, because I'd take all that extra energy home with me. I'd walk in the door, still feeling all revved up from the meeting, and I would just snap at Richard over the tiniest, most ridiculous little things. I mean, the poor man would just be sitting in his chair watching his programs, and maybe he’d left his boots too close to the front door or put a damp glass on the end table without a coaster—which, yes, drives me up the wall, water rings are an absolute menace to good wood—but normally I'd just sigh and wipe it up myself. 

But on those days? Oh, I would just bite his head right off. I'd lay into him about it, just snapping and fussing and making a mountain out of a molehill until he didn't know which way was up. It was like I had all this buzzing, electric energy inside me, and if I wasn't running the show and talking a mile a minute at the clubhouse, it just turned into me being terribly irritable and short-tempered with my husband at home. So, yes, I definitely have had periods like that where I was just running on a completely different engine than I am right now.
Thinking about those high-energy, 'on top of the world' periods you described—about how many days in a row would that heightened, revved-up feeling typically last before it settled back down?

Oh, heavens, how many days in a row... you know, I really couldn't give you a precise number if my life depended on it. I wish I had written it down in my day planner, right next to the street sweeping schedule or the trash pick-up days, but when you’re in the middle of feeling that... that electric, revved-up way, time just sort of slips right through your fingers. 

It’s not like these awful foggy spells I'm in right now where every single hour drags on like a month and you’re just staring at the clock ticking on the wall, waiting for the day to be over. No, when I had that fire lit under me, I was just moving from one thing to the next so fast. I’d be sorting out the master keys, and then I'm off lecturing Mrs. Henderson at the meeting, and then I'm back home fussing at Richard about his boots and the water rings... and before I knew it, the days were just gone. 

I really couldn't tell you if it was just a couple of days or a longer stretch of them, because it all just blends together into this one big, busy, buzzing blur. You’d think I would notice, being a woman who has to track every single penny and every maintenance deadline for the entire complex, but my mind was just going a mile a minute. I was jumping from the parking rules to the landscaping issues to goodness knows what else, so I just didn't keep count of the days at all. I honestly just don't know.

Did Richard or anyone else ever comment that you seemed 'revved up' or different for several days in a row—like say, from one weekend to the next—or did it usually seem to resolve within just a day or two?

Well, Richard certainly had plenty to say about it, I can tell you that much. Because, you see... well, the timing of it all is really what brought everything to a head. This whole situation—this sharper change in my energy, all that bold confidence where I was just running the show and snapping at everyone, and then completely crashing right down into this awful, low, cloudy feeling I'm stuck in right now—this whole thing has been going on for right about two weeks. 

And I know it's been exactly two weeks because that is exactly when Richard officially retired. Thirty-five years he worked, and suddenly, just like that, he is home. All day. Every single day. And I am just not used to having a man underfoot from sunup to sundown, you know? I have had my routine for years and years. I get up, I go down to the clubhouse, I manage the property, and I used to come home to a nice, quiet house to collect my thoughts before he got off his shift. 

But now? Oh, heavens. He’s there when I wake up, he’s there when I pop home to check the mail, he’s sitting in his recliner asking what we’re having for dinner at two o'clock in the afternoon! So, yes, he absolutely noticed when I was all revved up, because I was just buzzing around him with all that sharp energy, telling him he needed to find a hobby or go build a birdhouse or go down to the hardware store—just anything to get him out of my kitchen while I was trying to clean. I was just so full of myself and so impatient with him just sitting there. And then, of course, right after that big burst of confidence, I just completely deflated into this terrible fog where I can barely look at an invoice. So it’s been this whole two-week ordeal, just this sharp up and then this terrible down, all starting the very minute he got his retirement watch and parked himself in my living room.

Can you recall if that revved-up, high-energy period lasted at least four days in a row—for example, did it span more than one weekend or continue through several consecutive workdays—before you noticed the crash into this current low mood?

Well, four days... you know, I hear what you're asking, doctor, I really do, but trying to pin down exactly four days right now is like trying to nail jelly to the wall. Because, like I was just saying, with Richard being home every single day now, the whole calendar has just gone completely out the window for me. 

It used to be I knew exactly what day it was without even looking. Tuesday was landscaping, Thursday was the trash bins, and the weekends were just for us. But now? Now every day feels like a Saturday, or maybe a Monday, because he's just always there in his slippers, asking me questions while I'm trying to think. So when I was all fired up and buzzing around, telling him to get out of my kitchen and snapping at him about the water rings... I mean, did that go on for a whole weekend and into the workweek? Did it last four days exactly? I just can't say for certain. 

It felt like one long, continuous stretch of me just running on pure nervous energy and him getting on my absolute last nerve, but whether that was three days or four days or five, I just couldn't swear to it on a stack of Bibles. Because before I knew it, all that fire just went out. It was like someone just pulled the plug right out of the wall. One minute I'm ready to reorganize the entire neighborhood watch and march down to the clubhouse, and the next I'm just sitting on the sofa, feeling like I'm made of lead and watching Richard flip through the daytime channels, not even caring if he leaves his boots right on the good rug. 

So I know it was a sharp change, and I know it all happened in this blur over the last two weeks since they gave him that retirement watch, but as for counting out exactly four days in a row for that revved-up part before the crash? I just don't have a clue, I really don't. The days just completely melted together on me.

During that revved-up, energetic period, did you notice needing much less sleep than usual—for example, waking up after just a few hours feeling fully rested—and if so, do you remember how many nights in a row that happened?

Sleep? Oh, well, that's another thing entirely, isn't it? Sleep has just been a completely foreign concept to me lately, and honestly, I don't know if I can give you a straight answer on how many nights in a row it happened, because the nights have just been as jumbled up as the days. 

You see, usually, I am very strict about my schedule. Lights out by ten-thirty, maybe a cup of chamomile tea if I'm feeling a bit restless, and I'm up at six sharp to get a head start on the property walk-through before the maintenance crew arrives. That's just how I've always done it. But during that time... when I had all that energy just coursing through me? Oh, heavens, it was like I didn't even need to close my eyes. I remember lying there in bed, and the clock on the nightstand—the one with the red numbers that Richard insists on keeping so bright—it would say two in the morning, and I would just be staring at the ceiling, wide awake. My mind would be racing, thinking about the new parking decals and how I needed to draft a letter to the residents in building C about their unauthorized patio furniture. 

And then, before I knew it, it would be four o'clock, and I'd just think, 'Well, what's the point of lying here?' So I'd get up. I'd be up at four in the morning, feeling like I'd just had a full eight hours, ready to tackle the day. I'd start cleaning the kitchen, scrubbing the grout, reorganizing the pantry—all while Richard was snoring away. And I felt completely fine! Not tired at all. I was just buzzing. 

But as for how many nights that went on? I really couldn't tell you. Did it happen three nights? Four? Maybe more? I just don't know. Like I said, everything just blurred together into this one long, continuous hum of energy. I was just going and going, and sleep just seemed like such a waste of time when there was so much to be done. But then, of course, the crash came, and now all I want to do is sleep, but even that feels heavy and awful. So, yes, I was definitely sleeping less and feeling rested, but counting the exact nights? I just can't do it, doctor. I really can't.

Is there any way to pin down the dates more precisely—for example, do you have calendar entries, text messages, or emails from that revved-up period, or could Richard recall specific days he noticed you acting that way?

Well, my calendar... yes, I suppose if you looked at my day planner, or maybe my email account, you could probably figure out the exact dates. Because, let me tell you, if you looked at the pages from those days, they are just scribbled black and blue with ink. 

You see, when I was feeling all revved up like that, I didn't just stick to my regular work. Normally I just handle the basics, you know, making sure the landscaping is done and the maintenance boys are doing their jobs. But suddenly... I just got it into my head that we needed to completely overhaul things. So I actually took on all these extra green-energy proposals. And I didn't just do it for my main property, oh no, I was doing it for several communities at the exact same time! 

I was just... I kept setting up calls and meetings with all these different contractors about solar panels and energy-efficient lights, even when my calendar was already completely full with my regular duties. I just kept cramming them in, double-booking myself, pacing around the kitchen island with the phone to my ear while Richard was sitting right there in his recliner trying to ask me about his lunch. 

So, yes, I imagine the emails are all sitting right there in my computer, and Richard would definitely remember the exact days I was carrying on about green energy and vendor bids.
